parsed.hook: The Brauneberger Juffer Sonnenuhr vineyard is a 40-degree slope of blue Devonian slate that faces due south, catching every photon of Mosel sunlight. Fritz Haag’s 2020 Auslese picks up the site’s signature flint strike and white peach, but the real story is the 20 g/l residual sugar that’s balanced by 9.5 g/l total acidity—sweetness that tastes like brightness, not syrup.
parsed.wine_summary: Fritz Haag farms 17 hectares in the middle Mosel, but the Juffer Sonnenuhr—an 18-hectare monopole within Brauneberg—is the crown jewel. The vineyard’s blue slate (Devonian, 380 million years old) fractures into thin plates that reflect heat and retain moisture, forcing vines to dig deep. This stress translates into Riesling with laser-like acidity and a mineral core that tastes like wet stone after rain. The Auslese designation here isn’t about cloying sweetness; it’s about concentration. In warm vintages like 2020, the extra hang time lets flavors develop while acidity stays razor-sharp. The Haag family has worked this site since 1920, and their winemaking—spontaneous fermentation in stainless steel, no fining—preserves the vineyard’s voice without gimmicks.
parsed.terroir_expression: The Juffer Sonnenuhr’s blue slate is softer than the red slate of the Saar or the hard gray slate of Bernkastel, which means it weathers into finer particles. This creates a soil that drains quickly but holds just enough moisture to sustain vines through dry spells. The vineyard’s steep pitch (up to 70% grade) forces roots to tunnel horizontally, picking up minerals that translate into a flinty, almost saline edge in the wine. The Mosel’s cool climate (average growing season temperature: 14°C) slows sugar accumulation, so even late-harvest Auslese grapes retain high acidity. The result is a wine that tastes both rich and electric—white peach and apricot jam on the palate, but with a finish that crackles like a struck match.
parsed.vinification_summary: Fritz Haag picks Auslese grapes in multiple passes, selecting only botrytized berries (noble rot) for this wine. Fermentation happens spontaneously with native yeasts in stainless steel tanks, a choice that preserves the grape’s aromatic precision. The wine is left on its lees for 6 months before bottling, which adds a subtle creaminess without masking the slate-driven minerality. One key technical note: the Mosel’s cool climate means malolactic fermentation is rare here—acidity stays tart and linear, unlike the rounder styles of warmer regions like the Pfalz.
